info.bio:
The Police surge en Londres en 1977, año de crispación, delincuencia y paro en el Reino Unido, causas del malestar social que hizo a la juventud comenzar a adorar a cuatro chavales que gritaban, despotricaban contra la monarquía y bebían mucha cerveza (y se metían lo que no era cerveza), Los Sex Pistols. En pleno auge del movimiento punk, en el que el virtuosismo instrumental y las letras carentes de insultos y política estaban relegados a un segundo plano, eran las bandas realmente buenas las que salían adelante. (Otro buen ejemplo de esta situación, además de los protagonistas de este texto, fueron Dire Straits)

Tres músicos tan brillantes como dispares componían The Police: Gordon Summer, más conocido como Sting, Stewart Copeland y Andy Summers (que sustituyó al guitarrista inicial, Henri Padovani, el cual no llegó a aparecer en ningún disco)
Tal mezcla podía, o llevar a un caos por falta de entendimiento entre el trío debido a las diferentes influencias e intenciones musicales de cada uno por separado, o sacar adelante un sonido propio y reconocible que les llevara a un abrumador éxito tanto para el público como para la crítica. Afortunadamente sucedió lo segundo, pero el precario equilibrio de poder y las tensiones entre sus miembros (particularmente dos de ellos) hicieron que la banda sólo publicara cinco discos antes de separarse.

Sting y Stewart Copeland fueron el embrión del grupo. El primero trabajaba como profesor  y tocaba el contrabajo en clubes y bares, además de tener un brillante talento para la composición comercial. Hay que decir que Sting es también un bajista subvalorado, con una gran capacidad y creador además de geniales líneas de bajo. Cualquier profesor o manual de bajo eléctrico lo señala como bajista recomendado. Recibió su apodo(que utiliza para todo,excepto para firmar documentos oficiales) durante uno de los ensayos del grupo(al que apareció con un jersey de rayas negro y amarillo).Stewart Copeland era un batería de rock progresivo que había comenzado a aporrear a principios de los setenta, pero que en realidad estaba enamorado del sonido reggae. Su particular forma de tocar la batería le ha encumbrado como uno de los mejores percusionistas del mundo.

A ellos se unió Andy Summers, experimentado guitarrista de jazz que ya había colaborado con grandes como Eric Burdon de The Animals. Diez años mayor que Sting y Stewart, casado y con una hija, Police era para Andy la última oportunidad de sacar tajada en el mundo de la música… y vaya si acertó.

Summers era la columna vertebral de la composición músical del grupo. En torno a sus riffs de guitarra arpegiados se adhería la curiosa y potente batería de Copeland y las letras y ritmos de Sting.

“Outlandos D’amour”, su primer trabajo, ya contenía clásicos instantáneos como So Lonely, Can’t stand losing you o Roxanne, en la que Sting habla sobre la vida de una prostituta. Un año después, con Reggatta de Blanc (cuyo significado es “el reggae de los blancos”), no hicieron sino consolidarse como una de las mejores bandas del momento. A estos les siguieron “Zennyata Mondatta”, “Ghost in the machine” y “Syncrhronicity”. (Más tarde editaron un directo)

Fue ya en Ghost in the machine, cuando las crecientes tensiones, principalmente entre Sting y Copeland, comenzaron a hacerse patentes. En las sesiones de grabación de este disco ya nadie quería bajar el volumen de su instrumento para sonar menos que los demás. Dichas tensiones ya eran totalmente públicas y conocidas con el lanzamiento de Synchronicity (la portada del disco es como un atisbo del futuro ya que aparecen los tres músicos agrupados cada uno en una franja de diferente color. El colmo fue una actuación en la que Stewart Copeland tocó con una camiseta que decía “Odio a Sting”… con estas señales no era difícil vaticinar lo que iba a ocurrir).

El grupo se disolvió cuando se encontraba en la cresta de la ola, tras la gira de Synchronicity en 1983. Este álbum que contenía el tema “Every Breath you take”, del que Mike Jagger reconoció que era la mejor canción de la historia junto con Satisfaction (modestia aparte de Jagger…)

El grupo se reunió en 1986, sacando una versión del tema “Don’t stand so close to me” y realizando una gira, pero volvió a disolverse ese mismo año. La última reunión se ha producido recientemente, como 30 aniversario del lanzamiento del primer disco de su primer disco de estudio

Sting, siguió su carrera en solitario, consiguiendo un más que notable éxito. Copeland ha trabajado como compositor de cine para directores como Oliver Stone o Francis Ford Coppola. Summers ha llevado una carrera más discreta y ha publicado hace poco varios libros sobre el grupo. . scenes.desc: El reggae se populariza en el Reino Unido con Prince Buster y Desmond Dekker; Jimmy Cliff lo casa con el «paz y amor» hippy y los Maytals le dan nombre. Los sound systems de los guetos convierten a los «selectors» en los verdaderos animadores: el «toasting» sobre los discos será tan importante como la música. Bob Marley y los Wailers lo llevan a Occidente; Burning Spear firma quizá su cima artística (Marcus Garvey). Los ingenieros remezclan las caras B quitando las voces: King Tubby inventa el dub usando la mesa de mezclas como un instrumento, y Lee Perry (Super Ape) y Augustus Pablo fijan el canon.

podcast.title: 1977 Breakthrough Sound
podcast.body: When The Police emerged in 1977, Stuart Copeland's drumming immediately distinguished itself from other New Wave drummers of the era. His snare drum was tuned very tightly, producing a sharp, high-pitched crack, and his playing incorporated a distinct reggae and dub feel, often expressed with rim shots. There was also a subtle Middle Eastern infusion blended with jazz, evident in his use of small, high-pitched splash cymbals, making him one of the first modern rock drummers to adopt them. He was also notable for his syncopated beats led from the hi-hat. "When they came along in 1977, he immediately stood out from all the other new wave drummers of the era."

podcast.title: Formation and Sound (1977)
podcast.body: When The Police emerged in 1977, their sound was unique, blending punky elements with pop sensibilities and an unusual reggae influence for the time. "When the police first showed up in 1977, they sounded like no one else. They were punky but tempered with pop. And they had this reggae thing going which was highly unusual for the day."

podcast.title: US Tour and CBGB Debut (1978)
podcast.body: In October 1978, Miles Copeland self-funded a tour of America for The Police, commencing in New York City. Their first performance was at the punk mecca CBGB, where they delivered an acclaimed, punk-worthy set at the notoriously grungy but hip club. "Miles Copeland had the clever idea to self-fund a tour of America for the police, starting in New York City. When they arrived in October of 78, their first stop was Punk Mecca CBGB. At the notoriously grungy but reliably hip club, the police played an acclaimed punk-worthy set."

podcast.title: Band's Peak and Internal Strife (1984)
podcast.body: After achieving significant success within just over five years of recording, The Police experienced intense internal exhaustion. The band was characterized by three headstrong personalities, and constant bickering was fueled by Andy Summers's and Stuart Copeland's envy of Sting's prolific and hit-packed songwriting. Even the band's producers found the tension exhausting. "The three headstrong personalities coupled with Andy Summers and Stuart Copeland's envy of Sting's prolific hit-packed songwriting led to constant bickering that even the band's producers found exhausting."

podcast.body: Sting, Andy Summers, and Stewart Copeland put together a full global reunion tour that played over 150 dates around the world through 2007 and 2008. The two-year trek was the third highest-grossing tour in history at the time and remains within the top 20 all-time. Despite some interpersonal dynamics, the three members "mostly got along" during the tour, even with Copeland critiquing their onstage mistakes online. "Then in 2007, Sting, Summers and Stuart Copeland put together a full global reunion tour that played more than 150 dates around the world through 2008."

podcast.body: The Police, a group historically known for internal disagreements, reunited for a tour in 2007 and 2008 due to an unprecedented financial offer from Live Nation's head of global touring, Arthur Fogel. The tour grossed $359 million, equivalent to $508 million in today's currency, showcasing the immense profitability of reunions driven by economic factors and fan nostalgia. "The police reunion tour of 2007 and 2008 grossed $359 million. That's $508 million in today's cash."

podcast.body: In 2025, Sting's bandmates, guitarist Andy Summers and drummer Stuart Copeland, initiated a lawsuit against Sting, seeking arranger's fees they claim are owed for "Every Breath You Take." They argue that their instrumental contributions were vital to the song's distinctive sound and enduring popularity, drawing a parallel to DJ Stonebridge's lack of recognition for "Show Me Love." "Stings to police bandmates, guitarist Andy Summers and drummer Stuart Copeland have sued Sting for what they say they are owed for a ranger's fees on every breath you take."

xref.title: Munich Bar Brawl and Aftermath (2002)
xref.body: On December 1st, 2002, during a tour supporting "Heathen Chemistry," Liam Gallagher, Alan White, and two other band members became heavily intoxicated at the Bayer Sherhoff hotel bar in Munich, Germany. They provoked five Italians by throwing peanuts, and after an Oasis song played, Liam and Alan White jumped on stage for "unwanted karaoke." A fight erupted after one of them jumped on a table, causing it to collapse. The brawl escalated into the hotel lobby, resulting in broken furniture and smashed windows. Police arrived with ten cars to find Alan White bleeding from an ashtray to the head, and security details injured, one unconscious. Liam lost several teeth and was bruised, and was arrested after kicking a police officer. Toxicology confirmed his extreme intoxication and the presence of cocaine. Liam required $30,000 in emergency dental surgery, and he and two band members spent 12 hours in jail. The rest of the European tour was canceled, costing millions in revenue, and management paid over $300,000 for Liam to leave Germany. Noel, who was in his room during the incident, was furious upon learning of it. Liam could have faced two years in jail. "Liam had lost several teeth and was bruised and battered all over. The police spokesman was quoted as saying, the boy didn't look good. Several of his teeth were punched out. But that didn't stop him from launching himself at one of the cops kicking him in the ribs as hard as he could."

xref.title: Death by Suicide (May 18, 2017)
xref.body: Chris Cornell died by suicide by hanging on May 18, 2017, at 1:30 AM, a death that came as a "real shock" to many. He was found in his hotel room (room 1136 at the MGM Grand, Detroit) with a red exercise band around his neck, attached to a carabiner jammed tightly into the doorframe. The night before, May 17, Soundgarden played a show at the Fox Theatre in Detroit, after which his long-time tour manager felt Chris was "messed up and struggling." Back at the hotel, his bodyguard, Martin Kirsten, gave him two Ativan pills, for which Chris had a prescription. Shortly after, Chris spoke to his wife Vicki, who noted his slurred speech; he claimed to have taken "too much Ativan" and was "just tired." He abruptly hung up, alarming Vicki. Martin Kirsten, called by Vicki, found Chris's room latched from the inside. After kicking open both the room and bathroom doors, he found Chris. The toxicology report found Ativan (four doses), pseudoephedrine, butylbital, caffeine, and Narcan (administered by paramedics). While his wife speculated drugs contributed to an "altered mental state," the police ruled it suicide by hanging. "Chris was pronounced dead at 1.30, and the police ruled a suicide by hanging."

xref.title: Dream Machine Connection Myth
xref.body: A cult-like organization called "Friends Understanding Kurt" suggests that Kurt Cobain's death in 1994 was linked to his use of a "dream machine," a trance-inducing device invented by William Burroughs. After their 1992 collaboration, Burroughs was reportedly pleased and told Kurt about the machine, even introducing him to builder Dave Woodward in San Francisco. Kurt immediately ordered one, but Courtney Love, sensing its danger, tried to prevent its delivery. According to "Friends Understanding Kurt," Cobain used the machine for up to 72 hours at a time, and it was found just 20 feet from his body on April 8, 1994, though neither police nor the coroner investigated this connection. "The machine was found just 20 feet away from his dead body on April 8, 1994. Neither the police, nor the corner investigated the connection."
